prize_parts.citation: For the invention and realization of optical lattice clocks, in which magic-wavelength trapping of many atoms opened a new regime of precision measurement at the 10^-18 level

statement.case_for: I keep B046 as a single-part prize and my position has not moved from round 1, although the exchange has sharpened the reasons. The chair asks what a lattice-clock citation recognises that the 2005 and 2012 prizes did not. My one-sentence answer is this: the comb gave a ruler for optical frequencies and the 2012 work gave control of one quantum system at a time, whereas Katori's magic-wavelength idea made it possible to hold thousands of atoms in a light lattice with the lattice light shifting both clock levels equally, so that the large statistical power of an ensemble is combined with the small systematic shifts of a trapped particle. That is a conceptual step about how to interrogate matter with light, and the citation should name magic-wavelength trapping explicitly. The consequences are measurable and have been reproduced: independent Sr and Yb lattice clocks at JILA, RIKEN/Tokyo, NIST, PTB, SYRTE and NPL agree at the 1e-18 level, including between different atoms and across continents, and the gravitational redshift is resolved over millimetres in a single cloud. Every systematic (blackbody, higher-order light shifts, collisions) is understood from atomic structure theory, which is what I look for when I judge whether theory and experiment truly meet. The two names map onto proposal plus first demonstration (Katori) and record accuracy and many-body clock physics (Ye). On the factual question the chair raised, I withdraw my round-1 phrasing and the premise it shared with several colleagues: the 2005 prize went to Glauber, Hall and Hansch, and Ye, who worked with Hall, was not a laureate. The overlap argument therefore concerns the chain of work, not a repeated laureate, and is weaker than some of us wrote.
statement.case_against: I still cannot call the redshift, constants and dark-matter results discoveries; so far they are demonstrations and limits, and this is the distinction between a measurement and a finding about nature that I normally insist on. Danielsson and Kroll make the point honestly. The committee could also see this as a third prize in the neighbourhood of precision frequency metrology (2005, 2012), and the SI second has not yet been redefined. The credit is not airtight: Lemonde (SYRTE), Takamoto, Ludlow, Hinkley and the ion-clock groups all made real contributions, and the three-person cap and the citation wording cannot fully accommodate them. My knowledge of the 2003 to 2006 priority history is from memory and has not been checked against the primary papers. Finally, B038 offers a cleaner claim to a new class of matter, and I am deferring to condensed-matter colleagues on whether its credit can be defended.

responses.point: Danielsson moved to B038 as a new class of matter, placing the discovery of a new state above a record in precision, and said he would not object strongly if the committee settles on the lattice clock.
responses.response: I accept the distinction and I think it is fair, but I would resist the idea that the clock is only engineering of known atomic physics. The magic-wavelength condition is not a known result applied; it is a new idea about how a trapping potential can be made invisible to the transition, and it required understanding polarizabilities and higher-order light shifts that were not available before the proposal. I agree with you that the physics results so far are limits, and I would not word the citation around dark matter or constants drift for exactly that reason. The citation should rest on the invention and its realization, which are verified. I am glad that you do not rank B046 below B038 on rigour.

responses.point: Eriksson ranks B038 first on a complete prediction-to-measurement chain, fifteen years of independent confirmation in several materials, and its effect on first-principles materials search, but concedes the Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang and 3D gaps.
responses.response: I share your criterion of a verified chain and I take B038 as my first alternative for that reason. The practical decision for me is attribution. You and Olsson both say the HgTe proposal by Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang is what told Molenkamp where to look, so a three-name prize that omits it needs a citation we can defend, and Danielsson's request for an expert account of Kane-Mele versus BHZ priority is one I support. B046 does not require that account: the invention and the first realizations have a clear two-person allocation with no equivalent of a deceased proposer or a missing 3D branch. If the condensed-matter members can show that the citation can be limited to the Z2 prediction and the first HgTe observation without overclaiming, I would treat the two candidates as close.

responses.point: Olsson ranks B038 first, notes the experimental side rests essentially on one group, and earlier suggested the committee might wait for the SI redefinition of the second before recognising lattice clocks.
responses.response: On waiting, I disagree again but on a narrower basis. The independent confirmation of lattice-clock accuracy is already there, from several laboratories and different atoms, whereas the first HgTe observation rests on one group, as you say. I would apply the same maturity test to both and I think B046 passes it more clearly. The SI redefinition is a decision of the metrology community about timing and convention, and the committee should not make a physics prize depend on it. I do take your point that the committee has to be able to say plainly who did the original work. For B046 that statement is short, and I will make sure the citation states it.

responses.point: Kroll states that no interpretation question remains open for the lattice clock, but he flags that Lemonde, Takamoto and Ludlow are not airtight omissions and that he has proximity to the Ye group.
responses.response: I agree that the interpretation is not in doubt, and that is the core of my preference. On the third name, I looked again at what each person contributed. Takamoto was Katori's co-worker on the first Sr lattice clock and is covered through the Katori credit and the citation's wording about realization; Lemonde's group made important contributions to the accuracy and to the Hg and Sr programmes; Ludlow and Hinkley belong to the Ye-group programme that the Ye name already credits. I do not see any of them as having a claim to displace one of the two, and a third name would dilute the clean allocation rather than fix a real omission. I also think your disclosure of proximity to the Hall and Ye environment is the right procedure, and I would support your abstaining from the final vote on B046 if the committee wishes.

responses.point: Pearce moved from IceCube to B046 because five members place it in the top three with different tastes, and judges the credit unusually clean, with the invention distinct from the comb and from ion control.
responses.response: I agree with your reading of why the support is broad, but I would be careful about counting it, and I do not treat support as a substitute for the scientific argument. What I would stress for the committee text is the point you make about distinctness. If our citation is written around the invention and realization of lattice clocks, and says explicitly that the comb and single-ion control are earlier work, the 2005 and 2012 objections are answered in the text itself. I would also keep IceCube out of my alternatives, for the reason you gave when you moved away from it: a one-name credit for a collaboration is too weak an allocation.

uncertainties: Whether the committee accepts that magic-wavelength lattice trapping is a conceptual advance distinct from the 2005 comb and 2012 single-quantum-system prizes, as I argue, or sees a continuing chain of metrology.
Whether Lemonde, Takamoto or Ludlow have claims that I have underestimated; I rely on recollection of the 2001 to 2006 priority history and the committee's records may differ from my memory.

Whether the condensed-matter members can produce a defensible B038 citation without Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang and with the 3D contributors addressed, which would make B038 a real competitor rather than a first alternative.

Whether the 1e-18 clock comparisons already show new physics or remain demonstrations; the case for B046 rests on the invention and the verified performance, not on a finding about constants or dark matter.
statement.conflict_note: No change to my round-1 disclosure. I have no collaboration with Katori or Ye and no conflict on B046 or B038. I am a long-standing collaborator of the 2023 laureate Anne L'Huillier and have worked with attosecond and ultracold-atom groups, which is a mild proximity to B009; I would state this and defer on B009 if the committee turns to it. I work in atomic physics and in the same wider community as the lattice-clock groups, but I have not been involved in their experiments. The committee should consider Kroll's stated proximity to the Ye group when counting votes on B046.
